FIRE · 2025

On the Unwashed Masses and Their Lack of Vision

2 September 2025·3 min read·628 words

Archived verbatim. Published 2 September 2025 on Medium, in the Fire era — before Brad Devices shipped anything. The prose is the record and is not edited here; corrections go in a new essay.

• People ask me, "Bradley, why can’t other people do what you’re doing?" And I just look at them and want to laugh. Bless their little hearts. They think this is about coding or building circuits. It’s not. That’s the easy part. A chimp with enough time and a good C++ manual could probably get a basic OS to boot. The hard part is the obsession.
• You know what they want? A "chill life." They want to clock in, collect a paycheck, and go home to watch Netflix. They want to buy a lifestyle, not build a legacy. I’m over here eating microchip schematics for breakfast—and no, that’s not a joke, my doctor is worried—while they’re trying to figure out if they should get the pumpkin spice latte or the regular one. They want success without the fever dream. They want to be a "visionary" on their LinkedIn profile, but they get a paper cut from a blueprint and suddenly they need a "mental health day." Please. My mental health day is when I successfully debug a line of code that’s been haunting me for a week. That’s my version of a tropical vacation.
• This isn’t just about building a device; I’m building a technocratic mythos. I’m not just making a console, I’m making a legend. When people see my console, I don’t want them to just see a piece of plastic and metal. I want them to see the lore, the emotion, the sheer madness that went into every single millimeter of it. This isn’t a job, it’s a love affair. And my dear friends, you’re not invited to the wedding.
On the Bloated Dinosaurs and Their Board Meetings
• Then there’s the other question: "Why can’t Google or OpenAI or Tesla just do this?" Oh, that’s my favorite one. You think they could, right? With all their money and all their brilliant minds? The truth is, they’re too fat and lazy.
• They’re like cruise ships—massive, slow, and scared of a little turbulence. They’ve got ten committees arguing about a logo font while I’m over here building a quantum mesh network that will obliterate their stupid ISPs. I’m a jet ski with rocket boosters. They’re busy making sure their balance sheets look good. I’m busy rewriting history.
They’re worried about profit margins and shareholder value. They want 5% more ad revenue. I want to build the next civilization. We’re not even playing the same game. They’re playing checkers; I’m playing a game of galactic chess they don’t even know exists. They have an image to protect. They can’t just come out and say, "Yeah, we’re going to plug this thing right into your brain via haptic gloves." I can say that. I did say that. And I trademarked it.
They think they have a monopoly on innovation. They don’t. They have a monopoly on bureaucracy. And that, my friend, is their biggest weakness. They’re so busy protecting their turf that they don’t see the new king building an empire right under their noses.
• The bottom line is, anyone can build. But only a few of us are "nuts enough to finish the blueprint." I’m not just playing the game. I’m rewriting the rules, building the board, and selling the game pieces to the entire damn planet. Everyone else is just trying to update their LinkedIn bios to "visionary" without ever sweating through a 72-slide internal deck on GPU thermal management. Pitiful.
I’m not ahead of my time. I’m the reason time exists. You’re welcome.
